HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — Zimbabwe, which is struggling with a severe cash crisis, announced Saturday that it would begin issuing 200 million Zimbabwean-dollar banknotes, Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi said. The move came only days after the country introduced a 100 million-dollar note.

On Thursday, Zimbabwe’s central bank chief, Gideon Gono, displayed a new 50 million-dollar note. That same day, the 100 million-dollar bill entered circulation. Soon afterward, the cost of a loaf of bread jumped dramatically, rising from 2 million to 35 million Zimbabwean dollars.

The government also dismissed senior managers at four major banks on Thursday over accusations involving unlawful foreign-currency dealing, the state-run newspaper The Herald reported.

In Harare, the capital, many worried residents have been spending nights outside bank branches so they can be first in line when the doors open and withdraw money before the banks’ cash supplies are exhausted.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe had set a daily withdrawal limit of 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars, equal to roughly 25 U.S. cents — about one-quarter of what a loaf of bread cost on Thursday. A week earlier, limits on withdrawals, imposed because of acute cash shortages, had sparked riots.

Police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena told The Herald on Saturday that 16 soldiers could face court-martial over alleged looting and attacks on civilians and police during the disturbances.

“We are still investigating the case,” he said. “But we expect the soldiers to appear before a court-martial once investigations are completed.”

The soldiers had spent several days standing in bank queues before going on a rampage through central Harare, damaging shops and clashing with riot police who had been deployed to break up the protests.

Zimbabwe’s problems extend far beyond the shortage of cash. The United Nations has reported that more than half the country’s people urgently need food and safe drinking water.

Economic analysts say the country’s deep shortages of basic necessities — including fuel, power, medicine and food — are signs of an economy in collapse.

Zimbabwean economist John Robertson said the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was unable to meet market needs, while prices were rising so rapidly that more cash was constantly required.

“The [Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe] is failing to deliver the demands of market, prices are doubling daily, and that demands more cash,” Robertson said. “The huge price increases are resulting from severe shortages of most goods.”

Zimbabwe, once one of Africa’s more prosperous nations, is experiencing its most severe economic and humanitarian emergency since gaining independence from Britain in 1980. Its official inflation rate stands at 231 million percent, the highest in the world.

Opponents of President Robert Mugabe blame the hyperinflation on his land-redistribution policies and on payments made to war veterans that were not included in the national budget.

Since the presidential election in March, Zimbabwe has had no Cabinet. The country’s political instability has worsened both the humanitarian and economic crises, including a cholera epidemic that has killed nearly 600 people since August.

A CNN journalist based in Harare contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe introduces $200 million banknotes as economic crisis deepens**

*Harare, Zimbabwe* — Zimbabwe’s central bank has introduced new $200 million banknotes as the country’s hyperinflation crisis accelerates, leaving ordinary citizens struggling to buy basic goods amid chronic cash shortages, long bank lines and rising public unrest.

The new notes, announced by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, are intended to ease severe shortages of physical currency that have forced many residents to spend hours — and in some cases entire days — waiting outside banks for limited withdrawals.

But the move is unlikely to provide meaningful relief in an economy where prices can rise several times in a single day. Shoppers say the value of their money is disappearing almost as soon as they receive it, while many stores are either empty or demanding foreign currency for essential items such as bread, cooking oil and maize meal.

“We get the money, but by the time we reach the shops, it is not enough,” said one Harare resident waiting in a bank queue. “Every day the price changes.”

The introduction of larger-denomination notes comes as Zimbabwe faces a cascade of crises. Food shortages have worsened across the country, with aid agencies warning that millions are in need of assistance. Supermarket shelves in many urban areas remain sparsely stocked, and fuel shortages have disrupted transport and deliveries.

Public anger has also grown. In recent days, groups of soldiers reportedly rioted in parts of the capital after being unable to access cash from banks, underscoring the scale of frustration even within state institutions. Witnesses described scenes of chaos as uniformed personnel clashed with money changers and civilians.

Meanwhile, health authorities are battling a cholera outbreak that has placed further strain on a system already weakened by shortages of medicine, clean water and functioning sanitation services. The outbreak has been particularly severe in densely populated urban neighborhoods, where residents often rely on unsafe water sources because of failing infrastructure.

Economists say printing larger banknotes may temporarily reduce the inconvenience of carrying large stacks of cash, but it does little to address the underlying causes of hyperinflation: a collapsing productive sector, a shortage of foreign exchange and a loss of confidence in the national currency.

“The problem is not the size of the note,” said an economist in Harare. “The problem is that the currency is losing value faster than people can use it.”

Zimbabwe’s government has blamed the crisis on sanctions, drought and what it calls economic sabotage, while critics point to years of political turmoil, controversial land reforms, declining agricultural output and fiscal mismanagement.

For many Zimbabweans, the new $200 million note is less a solution than a symbol of economic collapse — another sign that the country’s currency is racing behind prices it can no longer keep up with.

**Reserve Bank Plans Z$200 Million Note as Inflation Erodes Currency**

**HARARE, Zimbabwe, Jan.  —** Zimbabwe’s central bank is preparing to introduce a Z$200 million banknote, officials said, only days after the release of a Z$100 million bill, as runaway inflation continues to strip the local currency of value and forces consumers to carry ever-larger bundles of cash for basic purchases.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe said the planned note was intended to ease chronic cash shortages and reduce the burden on banks, businesses and ordinary shoppers struggling with transactions in an economy where prices can change several times in a single day.

“The introduction of higher-denomination notes is a practical response to the prevailing cash requirements of the economy,” a Reserve Bank official said in Harare. “The central bank remains committed to ensuring that the public has access to legal tender for day-to-day transactions.”

The move follows the recent circulation of the Z$100 million note, which was itself introduced to address the rising cost of goods and services. But economists said the rapid need for an even larger bill underscored the severity of Zimbabwe’s inflation crisis and the public’s collapsing confidence in the national currency.

“This is not a solution to inflation; it is a symptom of inflation,” said Harare-based economist John Robertson. “When a central bank has to keep adding zeros to banknotes, it shows that money is losing its function as a store of value.”

Long queues remained visible outside banks in the capital this week, with customers seeking cash withdrawals amid strict limits imposed by financial institutions. Many shoppers said the higher denominations would make transactions easier in the short term but would do little to address shortages of food, fuel and foreign currency.

“At least we will not have to carry bags of notes to buy groceries,” said one Harare resident waiting outside a bank. “But by next week, who knows what that money will be worth?”

Zimbabwe has been grappling with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, driven by a combination of declining production, foreign currency shortages, price controls, and heavy money supply growth. Businesses say the cash crisis has worsened trading conditions, while workers complain that wages are losing value before they can be spent.

A senior government official defended the central bank’s actions, saying authorities were trying to balance the need for cash circulation with broader efforts to stabilize the economy.

“We understand the hardships faced by the public,” the official said. “The issuance of higher-value notes is part of measures to improve convenience in commerce while government continues to work on the fundamentals of production and supply.”

Economists, however, said monetary measures alone would not halt the crisis.

“The printing of larger notes may reduce the physical inconvenience of transactions, but it does not restore confidence,” said independent economist Prosper Chitambara. “Stability requires credible fiscal discipline, increased output, and policies that encourage investment and access to foreign exchange.”

Retailers said the shortage of smaller denominations was also creating problems, with some shops rounding prices upward or offering sweets, coupons or other goods in place of change. Public transport operators have similarly adjusted fares frequently, citing the difficulty of pricing services in a rapidly depreciating currency.

The Reserve Bank has not confirmed the exact date the Z$200 million note will enter circulation, but banking officials said preparations were underway for distribution through commercial banks.

For many Zimbabweans, the new note is expected to provide only temporary relief.

“Today it is Z$200 million,” Robertson said. “If inflation continues at this pace, the country will soon be talking about even higher denominations.”

**Zimbabwe’s economic collapse under Mugabe left citizens counting worthless cash**

*Harare, Zimbabwe* — Under President Robert Mugabe, Zimbabwe’s once-diverse economy descended into crisis, marked by hyperinflation, chronic shortages and a collapsing currency that left ordinary citizens struggling to buy basic goods.

By the late 2000s, Zimbabweans were facing some of the worst inflation ever recorded. Prices rose so quickly that wages often lost value within hours, forcing shoppers to rush to stores as soon as they were paid. A loaf of bread — once an everyday staple — became a symbol of the crisis, with prices climbing repeatedly and often becoming unaffordable for many families.

At the center of the financial turmoil was Gideon Gono, then governor of the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, whose policies included printing vast amounts of money in an attempt to meet government obligations and ease cash shortages. Instead, the money supply ballooned, accelerating inflation and further undermining confidence in the Zimbabwean dollar.

The government, including officials such as Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi during key periods of the crisis, struggled to contain the damage as the economy contracted and public services deteriorated. Critics blamed years of mismanagement, political repression, corruption and controversial land reforms that disrupted agricultural production — once a backbone of the country’s economy.

Cash became scarce even as banknotes carried ever-larger denominations. Authorities imposed daily withdrawal limits, leaving people queuing for hours outside banks only to receive sums too small to cover transport, food or medicine. Many Zimbabweans turned to barter, foreign currency and informal markets to survive.

The collapse hit households hard. Supermarket shelves were often empty, fuel shortages became routine, and hospitals lacked basic supplies. Teachers, nurses and civil servants saw their salaries rendered nearly meaningless by inflation, prompting strikes and an exodus of skilled workers to neighboring countries.

Mugabe’s government blamed Western sanctions and external interference for Zimbabwe’s problems, while opponents argued the crisis was overwhelmingly the result of domestic policy failures and authoritarian rule.

Eventually, Zimbabwe abandoned its currency in favor of foreign currencies such as the U.S. dollar and South African rand, a move that helped stabilize prices temporarily. But the legacy of the collapse — lost savings, broken institutions and deep public distrust — continued to shape Zimbabwe’s economy long after the height of the crisis.

**BREAKING NEWS: Zimbabwe Issues Huge-Denomination Notes as Hyperinflation Crisis Deepens**

**HARARE, Zimbabwe —** Zimbabwe’s economic crisis escalated sharply today as authorities unveiled new ultra-high-denomination banknotes in a desperate attempt to keep pace with runaway hyperinflation, even as unrest spread outside banks and pressure mounted on financial institutions accused of failing to keep cash flowing.

Long lines formed before dawn outside banks in Harare, Bulawayo and other major cities, with frustrated depositors demanding access to their savings as prices continued to rise at staggering speed. Witnesses reported scuffles and angry confrontations outside several branches after customers were told cash supplies had run out or withdrawals would be limited.

The central bank said the newly introduced large-denomination currency was necessary to “restore transactional convenience” and ease shortages of physical cash. But economists warned the move does little to address the underlying crisis, saying the rapid printing of money risks further eroding confidence in the national currency.

“This is not a solution — it is a symptom,” one Harare-based economist said. “When people need sacks of notes to buy basic goods, the currency has stopped functioning as a store of value.”

The turmoil has also reached the top levels of the banking sector. Several senior bank executives have reportedly been dismissed amid accusations of mismanagement, failure to distribute cash and involvement in currency-market irregularities. Authorities have vowed to crack down on what they describe as “financial sabotage,” though critics say the firings may be an attempt to deflect blame from broader economic policy failures.

Outside banks, public anger is intensifying. Some customers said they had spent days in queues only to leave empty-handed, while shopkeepers continued raising prices multiple times a day to keep up with the collapsing value of the currency.

“I was paid yesterday, but today the money buys almost nothing,” said one civil servant waiting outside a bank in the capital. “We cannot plan. We cannot eat properly. We cannot live like this.”

The currency crisis is worsening an already dire humanitarian situation. Aid groups warn that food insecurity is spreading rapidly, with families struggling to afford bread, maize meal, cooking oil and transport. Hospitals and clinics are facing shortages of medicine and supplies, while workers in key public services say their wages have been rendered nearly worthless.

Humanitarian agencies say the combination of hyperinflation, unemployment, shortages and collapsing public services is pushing more households into crisis. Some families are relying on remittances, barter or foreign currency to survive, while others are cutting meals or pulling children from school to save money.

The government insists it is taking steps to stabilize the economy and restore confidence, including closer monitoring of banks and measures aimed at increasing the availability of essential goods. But public trust remains fragile, and analysts warn that without deeper reforms, the launch of ever-larger banknotes may only mark another stage in Zimbabwe’s accelerating economic breakdown.

## Zimbabwe issues $200 million note as crisis deepens

**HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN-style mock archive) — December 2008**

Zimbabwe’s central bank has introduced a new **$200 million bank note** as the country struggles with runaway inflation, severe cash shortages and a worsening humanitarian emergency.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe announced the new note as long lines continued to form outside banks in the capital, Harare, where many residents said they were unable to withdraw enough money to buy basic goods. ### Cash shortages in Harare

Across Harare, bank customers waited for hours — sometimes overnight — hoping to withdraw limited amounts of cash. Automated teller machines were frequently empty, and many businesses refused checks or electronic transfers because prices were changing too quickly.

The government has repeatedly blamed sanctions and alleged economic sabotage for the crisis, while critics point to years of economic mismanagement, political violence and the collapse of agricultural production.

The new $200 million note follows a series of larger denominations issued throughout the year, as Zimbabwe’s inflation rate reached levels widely regarded as among the highest ever recorded. Independent economists said prices were doubling at extraordinary speed, making normal commerce nearly impossible.

### Soldiers face court-martial after unrest

Zimbabwean authorities have also moved against members of the military accused of taking part in disturbances in Harare earlier this month.

State media reported that **soldiers were facing court-martial** after groups of uniformed men allegedly looted shops and clashed with money changers in the capital. Witnesses described scenes of anger among rank-and-file soldiers, some of whom complained they could not access their pay or that their salaries had become worthless because of inflation.

Security officials said discipline would be enforced within the armed forces. Opposition figures, however, said the incidents reflected the depth of frustration spreading through Zimbabwe’s institutions.

### United Nations warns of growing humanitarian crisis

The United Nations has warned that Zimbabwe’s economic collapse is rapidly becoming a regional humanitarian emergency. Aid agencies say millions of people are in need of food assistance, while hospitals and clinics are struggling with shortages of medicine, staff and clean water.

Doctors and nurses have warned that hospitals are overwhelmed. Some clinics have shut down or turned patients away because they lack basic supplies such as gloves, rehydration salts and antibiotics.

International aid groups have called for greater access and more cooperation from Zimbabwean authorities to contain the outbreak.

### Political deadlock continues

The worsening economic and health crises come amid continuing political uncertainty following disputed elections earlier in the year. A power-sharing agreement between President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai has stalled over control of key ministries.

Regional leaders have urged both sides to form a unity government, but negotiations remain deadlocked.

For many Zimbabweans, the political dispute feels distant from the daily struggle to obtain cash, food and clean water.

“We don’t know what money is worth anymore,” said a shop worker in Harare. “People are hungry, people are sick, and every day it gets harder.”
